cards.definition: One measurable input column that describes each example.
cards.useCase: Choose features that carry information about the target.
cards.example: Floor area, bedrooms and age of a house

cards.definition: A quantitative feature that can take any value on a smooth scale, decimals included.
cards.useCase: Spot it by asking whether a value halfway between two others makes sense.

cards.definition: A feature with separate, countable values, usually whole numbers.
cards.useCase: Counts are discrete but still quantitative: you can add and average them.

cards.definition: A feature that names a category or quality instead of measuring an amount.
cards.useCase: Needs encoding before a model can use it. Either ordinal or nominal.

cards.definition: A qualitative feature whose categories have a meaningful order.
cards.useCase: The order can be kept when encoding; the gaps between levels are not measured.

cards.definition: A qualitative feature whose categories are names with no order.
cards.useCase: Encode it so that no category looks bigger than another, for example with one-hot.

cards.definition: The pandas marker for a missing or undefined value ('not a number').
cards.useCase: Find it with df.isna().sum() before deciding how to handle it.
cards.example: A blank survey answer loaded as NaN

cards.definition: Remove every row that has a missing value in any column: df.dropna().
cards.useCase: Good when few rows have gaps and many complete rows remain.

cards.definition: Remove a column that has missing values: df.dropna(axis=1) or drop it by name.
cards.useCase: Good when most of a column is empty and it adds little.

cards.definition: Filling a missing value with an estimate instead of removing the row.
cards.useCase: Use it when removal would lose too much data or bias what is left.
cards.example: Replacing a missing age with the median age

cards.definition: Replace gaps with the column average.
cards.useCase: Simple, but outliers pull it. It leaves the mean unchanged and shrinks the spread.

cards.definition: Replace gaps with the middle value of the column.
cards.useCase: Prefer it when there are outliers or skew.

cards.definition: Replace gaps with the most frequent value.
cards.useCase: Works for discrete numbers and for categories.

cards.definition: Replace gaps with a fixed value, or with a randomly picked existing value.
cards.useCase: Quick, but a constant such as 0 can pass for real data, so pair it with a missing indicator.

cards.definition: A new 0/1 column that records which rows had a missing value.
cards.useCase: Keep it next to the filled column when the fact of being missing may predict the target.

cards.definition: Put the most common category into every gap.
cards.useCase: The default fill for a categorical column, since words have no mean or median.
cards.example: Fill a missing city with the most frequent city

cards.definition: Copy the previous row's value into the gap. 'pad' is the same as ffill.
cards.useCase: Use it only when the row order is meaningful, such as days in a row.
cards.example: Red, NaN, NaN, Blue -> Red, Red, Red, Blue

cards.definition: Copy the next row's value upward into the gap (bfill).
cards.useCase: Same condition as forward fill; it can fill what a forward fill leaves in the first row.
cards.example: Red, NaN, NaN, Blue -> Red, Blue, Blue, Blue

cards.definition: Fill gaps with one fixed label, or a randomly chosen existing category.
cards.useCase: A label such as 'Unknown' keeps the gap visible as its own category.

cards.definition: Turning a continuous numeric feature into a limited set of ranges or categories.
cards.useCase: Simplifies a feature and softens noise, at the cost of detail.

cards.definition: Replace each value with the bin (range) it falls into. An example of discretization.
cards.useCase: Use it to turn numbers into ordered categories.

cards.definition: Bins that each cover the same size of range: (max - min) / number of bins.
cards.useCase: Easy to explain; an outlier can leave most rows in a few bins. pd.cut.

cards.definition: Bins that each hold about the same number of rows, cut at quantiles.
cards.useCase: Keeps the bins balanced even with outliers. pd.qcut.

cards.definition: Binning with one threshold: values on one side become one group and the rest another.
cards.useCase: Use it when a single cut-off is meaningful; you choose the threshold.
cards.example: Views of 5,000 or more: popular, else unpopular

cards.definition: Converting categories into numbers. All data must ultimately be numeric.
cards.useCase: Required before most models can use a categorical feature.

cards.definition: Map a two-value feature to 0 and 1.
cards.useCase: Use it for yes/no style features.

cards.definition: One 0/1 column per category, with a 1 in the row's own category.
cards.useCase: Use it for 3+ nominal categories: it adds no false order. pd.get_dummies.
cards.example: red, green, blue -> is_red, is_green, is_blue

cards.definition: Replace each category with a statistic of the target for it, usually the mean.
cards.useCase: Use it for features with very many categories. Learn it from training data only, to avoid leakage.

cards.definition: Rescaling features to comparable ranges so large values do not dominate.
cards.useCase: Matters for distance-based models such as kNN; trees mostly do not need it.

cards.definition: (x - min) / (max - min): rescales values to run from 0 to 1.
cards.useCase: Use it when you need a fixed range; one outlier squeezes the rest.

cards.definition: (x - mean) / standard deviation: rescales to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
cards.useCase: No fixed range, so an outlier does not squeeze the rest, though it still shifts the mean and spread.

cards.definition: Min-max is squeezed by an outlier; neither method removes skew because both are linear.
cards.useCase: Use a log transform to reduce skew, and fit scalers on training data only.
cards.example: Salary with a few huge values

cards.definition: Min-max for unknown or non-bell-shaped data, kNN and neural networks; standardization when the algorithm assumes normal data.
cards.useCase: Decide from the distribution and the algorithm.

cards.definition: Divide the data into a training set to learn from and a test set held back.
cards.useCase: Generally 80% train and 20% test.

cards.definition: How well a model's performance carries over to unseen data.
cards.useCase: Judge it by comparing training and test accuracy.

cards.definition: The model memorizes the training data: high training accuracy, much lower test accuracy.
cards.useCase: Fix with a simpler model, fewer features, more data or cross-validation.

cards.definition: The model is too simple: low accuracy on both training and test data.
cards.useCase: Fix with a more flexible model or better features.

cards.definition: A table of actual versus predicted classes: true and false positives and negatives.
cards.useCase: Accuracy is the diagonal over the total; a false negative is a missed positive.

cards.definition: Split into k folds, use each as the test set once, and average the scores.
cards.useCase: Gives a steadier estimate than one split and helps tune settings.
cards.example: 5 folds of 200 rows: 40 test, 160 train per round

cards.definition: Problems that grow as the number of features increases: sparse data, similar distances, cost.
cards.useCase: Explains why more features can hurt, especially for kNN.

cards.definition: With many features the same rows are spread thinly through a huge space.
cards.useCase: A reason a model can memorize noise instead of learning a pattern.

cards.definition: More features mean more training time, memory and a harder model to interpret.
cards.useCase: Cut the cost with feature selection or dimensionality reduction.

cards.definition: Keeping a useful subset of the original features and dropping the rest.
cards.useCase: Reduces dimensionality while the columns keep their meaning.

cards.definition: Scores features with simple criteria, such as correlation, before any model is trained.
cards.useCase: Cheapest approach; ignores how features work together.
cards.example: Drop features with near-zero correlation with the target

cards.definition: Trains a model on feature subsets repeatedly and uses an evaluation metric to choose.
cards.useCase: Tends to find a good subset for that model but is the most expensive.

cards.definition: Uses the results of a model, such as coefficients or importances, to choose features.
cards.useCase: Cheaper than a wrapper; depends on the model used.

cards.definition: Wrapper methods: forward adds one feature at a time, backward removes one at a time.
cards.useCase: Each step is scored by training a model, so they are effective but slow.
cards.example: Add the feature that raises the score most

cards.definition: A feature whose values barely differ between rows.
cards.useCase: A filter can drop it, since it is unlikely to help predict the target.
cards.example: A column that is 99% the same value

cards.definition: A number from -1 to 1 for the straight-line link between two variables.
cards.useCase: Judge by size: -0.85 is as strong as +0.85. Near 0 means little linear link.
cards.example: 0.02 with the target: candidate to drop

cards.definition: A table of correlations between every pair of features.
cards.useCase: Two features near 1 are redundant, so keep one.

cards.definition: A univariate filter that scores each feature against the target and keeps the k highest.
cards.useCase: Quick selection; it misses features that only help in combination.

cards.definition: Builds fewer new, uncorrelated features that keep as much variance as possible.
cards.useCase: Dimensionality reduction by transformation. Unsupervised: it ignores the target.

cards.definition: A new feature that is a weighted blend of the originals. The first points along the greatest variance.
cards.useCase: Components are perpendicular and ordered by the variance they explain.

cards.definition: The share of the total variance that each component captures.
cards.useCase: Add them up until you reach a target such as 90% to pick how many to keep.

cards.definition: Selection keeps some original columns unchanged; PCA creates new columns from combinations.
cards.useCase: Choose selection for interpretability, PCA to compress strongly correlated features. Standardize before PCA.
cards.example: Keep 'age'; or use a blend of 'age' and 'income'
